newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Sailors saved, but solo race safety questioned.
newsitem.headline: Sailors saved, but solo race safety questioned.

text.p: Australia was basking in the glow of a successful international rescue operation on Thursday after its navy plucked two European solo sailors from stormy seas off Antarctica.
But the drama highlighted the perils of round-the-world racing and yacht design and was expected to put pressure on the organisers of such races to pay more attention to safety.
Plaudits flowed in from France and Britain after first Thierry Dubois and then Tony Bullimore were saved -- in Bullimore's case seemingly against all odds.
"I think that's an absolutely extraordinary story," said British Prime Minister John Major, currently in India, when he heard of the rescue.
"I believe we owe a lot of thanks to the people who did it. I think very few people expected this happy outcome and I'm absolutely delighted to hear about it."
Bullimore, a 56-year-old said to be a former British Royal Marine, survived almost five days in an air pocket in the hull of his upturned yacht after the keel snapped off.
Dubois, who capsized in wild seas on Sunday like the Briton, had been drifting in a life raft since Monday.
Both were closer to Antarctica than Australia, chasing strong winds and the shortest route around the globe.
"It's an absolute Houdini act," said Australian Maritime Safety Authority spokesman David Gray. "This is one of the greatest all-time search-and-rescue efforts, there's no doubt about it."

Another French sailor in the Vendee Globe race, Raphael Dinelli, was rescued with Australian navy help two weeks ago and race organisers said on Wednesday they had lost contact with Canadian sailor Gerry Roufs.

After a costly rescue operation two years ago involving another French sailor, Isabele Autissier, Australians questioned the cost involved in sending a navy frigate more than 2,000 km (1,200 miles), diverting an oil tanker and keeping rescue planes circling overhead.

Australian Sports Minister Warwick Smith said he had written to his French counterpart, Guy Drut, a former Olympic hurdling champion, asking him to help put pressure on sailing authorities to make racing safer.
"Australia has no doubts about its obligations under international conventions to rescue yachtsmen in difficulty," Smith wrote.

"However, these recent rescues...must call into question the organisation of such events. While I am not suggesting that such events not take place, there must be some reconsideration of the routes which competitors are permitted to take.
"Specifically, I would suggest competitors take a longer, more northerly and therefore safer route."
Some fellow solo yachtsmen, while marvelling at Bullimore's rescue, also questioned the race rules and yacht safety.
Perth sailor Jonathan Sanders, who has sailed solo around the world three times, said the rules of the race forced the yachts to sail too far south, putting them under pressure.
Other yachtsman have criticised the move to lighter materials in yacht design, which many say have sacrificed safety for speed.
Chay Blyth, the first man to circumnavigate solo the globe from east to west against prevailing winds and currents, said the design of yachts in the Globe Vendee was untested.

"The problem here is not the course or how far south they go, it is with the construction of the yachts," he was quoted as saying from New Zealand. "It is the design factor and how far they are pushing their boats."
But retired solo sailor Ian Johnston, a friend of Bullimore for 15 years, said there was no way to stop such races.
"You can't stop people climbing Mount Everest," he said. "This is the Everest of sailing."
